CLASS 35 · AGES 4–5 · 20 COUNTING LESSONS

Numbers, Counting & Early Math.

HOW THIS CLASS WORKS

Twenty numbers, one smiling fruit at a time.

Every number in this class has its own step-by-step lesson: open the counting card together, count the smiling fruit, say the number, follow the teaching steps, ask the questions and finish with something real to count in your own kitchen. The order is gentle: cards one to five fit on one hand, cards six to ten need both hands, and the teens repeat one quiet pattern — a full ten, plus some more.

One card a sitting is plenty; the whole class is a month of two-minute counting moments. The kitchen is the answer key, so practice arrives with every snack — and reaching twenty earns a celebration the whole family can hear.

Twenty counting cards, one picture each. Every lesson is right here on this page — the original artwork with a drawing canvas, and what the number means and how to count it for real, taught step by step.

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

One Apple — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson starts counting from the true beginning: one. Your child learns that "one" names a single whole thing, practices the slow point-and-say that all counting rides on, and goes hunting for ones around the house.

What is this?

One means a single thing, all by itself. One apple, one nose, one you. It is the smallest number we say, and every other number is simply more ones stacked together.

What does it mean?

Before a child can count to five, they need the idea of one: that a single object can be named with a number word. One is also the seed of one-to-one counting — one word for one thing, never two words for the same apple.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three ones: the word "one" said while touching a single thing; the numeral 1 spotted on doors, remotes and birthday candles; and the feeling that one is whole and complete — one biscuit is a real, honest amount.

Why this matters

Every later number is built from ones, so a wobbly "one" wobbles all of maths. Naming single things proudly also builds the counting habit itself: touch, say, move on.

What it teaches

One-to-one correspondence (one word, one touch), the idea that numbers name amounts, vocabulary for single and whole, and the confidence to announce a number out loud — the bravest counting move there is.

Words to learn

onesinglealonefirstwholeapple

Say this to your child

“"This is one apple. One is the number for a single, whole thing. Find one of something nearby — touch it and announce it: one!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "This is one apple. Just one — say it with me: one."
  2. Touch the apple on the card and say "one" slowly. Then touch the big black 1 at the top. One apple, one numeral — both are one.
  3. Play find-one: walk the room and place a finger on one thing at a time — one chair, one lamp, one nose. Each time, say "one" like an announcement.
  4. Hand over one of something real — one cracker, one spoon — and let your child claim it: "One!" Receiving one thing feels like owning the number.
  5. Finish with the one-body trick: one head, one tummy, one me. One is not lonely; one is complete.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 1 sits at the top, one smiling red apple with a green leaf sits underneath it, and the word "apple" is printed below — one numeral, one apple, one word, three ways to meet the same number.

Ask your child

"How many apples are on this card?" "Can you find one of something near you?" "What is one thing you always have one of?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "One apple!" "One nose — one me!" or the proud collector's line: "I found one. Just one."

Out in the real world

Ones are everywhere once you hunt: one sun, one moon, one front door, one tooth that just arrived. Point out single things on every walk this week and let your child be the one who names them.

Try it together

The one-and-only game: set out a small pile of snacks and ask for "one, please" — then hand exactly one and wait for the announcement. Reverse roles and let your child be the giver who counts out a single prize for you.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many apples? What does one mean? Show me one finger." One apple, a single thing, one finger up — counting has officially begun.

Parent tips

If your child counts "one, two" while touching a single apple, gently restart together — the one-word-one-touch rhythm matters more than being right. And resist giving two when they asked for one; the exactness is the lesson.

This lesson pairs with the One Apple flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Two Bananas — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches two as the number of pairs — shoes, ears, bananas leaning together. Your child counts one-and-then-one-more, matches twins around the house and discovers that two is the friendliest number there is.

What is this?

Two is one and one more. Two bananas lean side by side; two shoes wait by the door; two ears listen for bedtime. Anything that comes as a matched pair is hiding a two.

What does it mean?

Two is where counting becomes a story: one, then another one. It is also the number of matching — pairs belong together, and spotting "the other one" is real mathematical thinking about sameness.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three twos: the word "two" counted slowly across two things; the numeral 2 recognized on its card and in the wild; and the pair idea — two things that match, one for each hand, one for each foot.

Why this matters

Pairs are a child's first number pattern. Matching two identical things builds same-and-different thinking, and the one-more step from one to two is the engine that will later drive all counting.

What it teaches

Counting with one-to-one touches across two objects, matching and pairing, the plus-one idea (one and one more), body awareness through paired body parts, and early comparison: same or different.

Words to learn

twopairbothmatchtwinside by side

Say this to your child

“"Two bananas — one and one more. Lots of things come in twos: two shoes, two hands, two ears. Let us find the pairs hiding in our house."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Two bananas, leaning together like friends. Let us count them: one... two."
  2. Touch each banana once — left, right — and say one number per touch. Two touches, two words, two bananas.
  3. Hunt for pairs: two shoes, two socks, two sleeves, two eyes. Touch each part of the pair as you count it.
  4. Build a two: set out one cracker, then add one more. "One and one more is two!" Eat one and watch two fall back to one.
  5. End with the body count: clap two times, stomp two times, blink two eyes. Two lives in the body, not just on the card.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 2 stands over two smiling yellow bananas leaning side by side, and the word "bananas" is printed below — the pair drawn exactly the way pairs look in real life.

Ask your child

"How many bananas? What else comes in twos?" "Can you match these two socks?" "If we eat one banana, how many are left?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "One, two — two bananas!" "Shoes come in twos!" or the matcher's cry: "Here is the other one!"

Out in the real world

Pairs run through the whole day: two sleeves to put on, two handles on the drawer, two wheels on each side of the car, two wings on every bird outside the window.

Try it together

Pairs snap: scatter a few socks or cards face-up and race to find the matching two. Then the two-steps game — everyone in the house takes exactly two steps and freezes; two is surprisingly hard to obey, and that is the fun.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many bananas on the card? Show me two fingers. What did we add to one to make two?" Two bananas, two fingers, one more — the pair is learned.

Parent tips

Let one banana get eaten mid-count and treat it as the best question of the day: "Now how many?" Numbers that shrink and grow on demand stop being pictures on cards. Keep matching games to a handful of pairs — victory first, difficulty later.

This lesson pairs with the Two Bananas flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Three Oranges — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson makes three feel famous: the number of bears, pigs and bowls of porridge in every story ever told. Your child counts three oranges one by one, lines up threes at snack time and hears why stories love this number.

What is this?

Three is one, two, then one more — three oranges standing in a row. It is small enough to see in one look and big enough to feel like real counting.

What does it mean?

Three is the last number the eye can recognize instantly without counting, and the first that fills a proper line. It is also the storybook number: three wishes, three tries, three friends — three is how stories keep things memorable.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three threes: touch-counting three things in order without skipping; the numeral 3 spotted out in the world; and the story pattern — things in threes are everywhere, from bowls to billy goats.

Why this matters

Counting a small line of things in strict order trains the scanning eye that bigger numbers will need. And knowing that "three" is a story number gives the count a place to live: tonight's bedtime story becomes counting practice.

What it teaches

Ordered touch-counting left to right, instant recognition of small groups (subitizing), story memory and prediction, and the patience to finish a count before grabbing — three is long enough to require it.

Words to learn

threerowlinefirstnextlast

Say this to your child

“"Three oranges — one, two, three. Three is the storybook number: three bears, three little pigs, three wishes. Let us count three of something and make up our own three story."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Three oranges in a row. Let us count them the slow way."
  2. Touch each orange once, left to right: one, two, three. Then run the finger back and check — the row did not change.
  3. Say the story secret: "Three bears, three pigs, three wishes. Three is the number stories love. Tonight we will count the threes in our story."
  4. Line up three real things — three crackers, three cars, three spoons — and count them. Rearrange into a triangle and count again: still three.
  5. Finish with three jumps, three claps, three big breaths. Three is a number the whole body can act out.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 3 stands above three smiling oranges with green leaves in a neat row, and the word "oranges" is printed below — a proper little number line of fruit.

Ask your child

"How many oranges? Which one is first? Which is last?" "What three things happen in your favorite story?" "Can you hop three times?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "One, two, three!" "The three pigs!" or the beginning-middle-end discovery: "First this, then that, then the end — three things!"

Out in the real world

Threes hide in plain sight: traffic lights have three colors, stools have three legs, sandwiches get cut in three for sharing. Ask "does that come in threes?" at every stop this week.

Try it together

The three-act snack: choose three things for the plate, count them in, eat them in order — first, next, last. Then tell a three-sentence story together about the three oranges: where they grew, who found them, who ate them.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many oranges? What number do stories love? Show me three jumps." Three in a row, three bears, three hops — the storybook number is home.

Parent tips

When a count skips or doubles back, slide your own finger under each orange and count with them — helping the finger is kinder than fixing the voice. Story threes work best when your child supplies the silly bits; counting is sneaky when the story is funny.

This lesson pairs with the Three Oranges flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Four Strawberries — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson counts four the sturdy way: four strawberries in a row, four legs under the table, four paws on the cat. Your child learns that four is the number things stand on — and practices counting without skipping.

What is this?

Four is one more than three: four strawberries standing in a row. Four is also the number of corners on a window, legs on a table and paws on a dog — the number that holds the world up.

What does it mean?

Four marks the point where counting must be careful: three can be seen at a glance, but four usually asks for a finger and a voice working together. It is the first number where the counting order really gets practiced.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three fours: touch-counting four things without a skip or a repeat; the numeral 4 recognized on cards and clocks; and the corner-and-leg idea — square things and standing things come in fours.

Why this matters

Careful counting at four builds the discipline every bigger number needs: one touch, one word, no rushing. Fours are also everywhere in the house, which turns furniture into free counting homework.

What it teaches

Strict one-to-one counting on a longer line, corner and shape awareness, body-part counting on pets and toys, and self-correction — the skill of noticing "I counted that one twice" and starting over without tears.

Words to learn

fourstrawberriescountingsteadyrestarthunt

Say this to your child

“"Four strawberries — one, two, three, four. Four is the number of legs and corners: tables stand on four legs, dogs walk on four paws, and every window has four corners. Let us count the fours in our house."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Four strawberries in a row. Count with me — and touch each one."
  2. Count the strawberries slowly, one touch per word. If the count tangles, laugh and start again: restarting is what good counters do.
  3. Go on a four hunt under the table: count the table legs — one, two, three, four. Count the chair legs. Count a teddy's paws. Four keeps appearing.
  4. Find the fours with corners: a book, a cracker, a window. Trace all four corners with one finger and say four at the last one.
  5. Act it out: four stomps, four claps, four hops — then freeze like a table on four legs.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 4 stands over four smiling red strawberries with their green calyxes on top, lined up in a row, and the word "strawberries" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many strawberries? How many legs does our table have?" "How many paws does the dog have?" "Show me four corners on this book."

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Four strawberries!" "The table has four legs — I counted!" or the paws report: "Bunny has four paws, two and two."

Out in the real world

Fours hold up daily life: four wheels on the stroller, four burners on the stove, four place mats at the table. Bedtime is four o'clock hour territory too — count four books before lights out.

Try it together

The paw game: everyone walks on all fours like the dog, the cat, the bear — count the hands and knees touching the floor: one, two, three, four. Then the corners march: walk the four corners of the rug, counting each one as you land.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many strawberries? What stands on four legs? Show me the four corners of a book." Four berries, four legs, four corners — the sturdy number is learned.

Parent tips

If the same strawberry gets counted twice, make restarting a game, not a failure — "the counting gremlin got us, again from one!" A child who restarts cheerfully will count to a hundred one day. Keep the four hunt moving; furniture waits patiently.

This lesson pairs with the Four Strawberries flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Five Pears — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson lands on the first big milestone: five, a whole hand. Your child counts five pears laid out two and three, matches the count to their own five fingers and learns why five is the number counters stop and celebrate.

What is this?

Five is a whole hand: five pears on the card, five fingers on your hand. On the card the pears sit two on top and three below — the same five, arranged like a little picture frame of fruit.

What does it mean?

Five is the first number people use as a container: we say "give me a high five", we count fives on clock faces, we sort coins into fives. Seeing five as one group — a whole hand — is the first big step toward working with bigger numbers.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three fives: counting all five fingers on one hand by touching each fingertip; recognizing the two-rows shape of five (like the card's pears, like a dice five); and the idea that five can be a stop-and-turn-around point in any count.

Why this matters

The hand is every child's first calculator. Once five is solid, six to nine become "five and some more", and later the whole ten-frame system in school math stands on this exact card. Five is not just a number — it is a tool.

What it teaches

Finger counting as a visible number line, recognizing five arranged in rows, stopping and starting on command in a count, and the first feel for parts inside a whole: two and three live inside five.

Words to learn

fivehandfingershigh fiverowswhole

Say this to your child

“"Five pears, five fingers — five is a whole hand. Count your fingers with me: one, two, three, four, five. When you get to five, you have counted a whole hand, and that is a real milestone."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Five pears — and look at your hand: five fingers. Five is a whole hand."
  2. Count the pears one by one, then press your hand flat on the card: the count and the hand match.
  3. Point at the arrangement: two pears on top, three below. Count the top row, then the bottom, then all five. Same five, two rows — that is a magic trick numbers can do.
  4. Give the hand a job: hold up five fingers, wiggle them one at a time and count each. Now hide two behind your back: "How many came with me?"
  5. Celebrate properly: five is the counting finish line everyone knows. High five, then count the five fingers on the high-five hand.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 5 sits over five smiling green pears — two pears in the top row and three in the bottom row — and the word "pears" is printed below, the five drawn in the same two-row shape as fingers spread on a hand.

Ask your child

"How many pears? How many fingers on one hand?" "If I hide two pears, how many are still there?" "What two rows make the five on the card?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Five pears — a whole hand!" "Two and three!" or the milestone announcement: "I counted all five by myself."

Out in the real world

Fives rule the house: five toes on each foot, five spots on a die, five days until the weekend. Set the table for five spoons, count five buttons on a coat, and clap a high five as the reward for every good count.

Try it together

Hand-stack towers: build a block tower, count to five blocks, then compare it to your spread hand — same five. Then the five-steps game: take exactly five giant steps, freeze, turn around and take five back.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many pears? Show me five. What two rows make the five?" Five pears, five fingers, two and three — the hand number is claimed.

Parent tips

Always count fingers by tapping each fingertip — the touch keeps slow counters from racing ahead. If your child spots the two-and-three split on their own, make a enormous fuss: seeing parts inside numbers is the whole future of arithmetic showing up early.

This lesson pairs with the Five Pears flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Six Grapes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson crosses the first frontier: six, the number that needs more than one hand. Your child counts six grapes in two neat rows, discovers five-and-one-more, and learns that bigger numbers are just old numbers wearing new sizes.

What is this?

Six is five and one more. On the card, six smiling grape bunches sit in two rows of three — the same shape as the six face on a dice. It is the first number that will not fit on a single hand.

What does it mean?

Once counting passes five, the hand becomes a helper: count five, then keep going. Six also arrives with its first real pattern — two rows of three — and patterns are what make big numbers friendly.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sixes: counting six things even when one hand runs out; spotting the two-rows-of-three shape (the dice six); and the plus-one bridge — five fingers plus one finger up equals six.

Why this matters

Six is where children either relax into counting or start to fear it, so this lesson keeps it playful: the hand runs out, everyone laughs, and the count simply carries on. The dice shape they meet here returns in every game they will ever play.

What it teaches

Counting past a handful, recognizing dice and row patterns, splitting numbers into parts (five and one, three and three), and the flexibility to keep a count alive when the tools run out.

Words to learn

sixdicerowsmore thanfive and onebunch

Say this to your child

“"Six grapes — five fingers and one more. Look, the grapes sit in two rows of three, the very same six that lives on a dice. Six is the first number that needs a helper hand."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Six grapes — more than one hand can hold! Let us count and find out."
  2. Count all six, touching each bunch. When the hand fills up at five, hold up the other hand for number six: "Six needs a helper finger!"
  3. Read the shape: two rows of three. Count the top row, count the bottom row, count them all: three and three make six — just like the six on a dice.
  4. Prove it with snack: line up six grapes like the card. Eat one and count what is left — five! Add it back — six again.
  5. Roll a dice if you have one: find the six face, match it to the card, and shout six together.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 6 sits over six smiling purple grape bunches arranged in two rows of three, and the word "grapes" is printed below — the exact pattern of the six face on a dice.

Ask your child

"How many grapes? Which hand ran out of fingers?" "How many rows? How many in each row?" "Can you find the six on this dice?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Six needs two hands!" "Three and three!" or the dice discovery: "The six looks just like our card!"

Out in the real world

Sixes wait in the kitchen and the game shelf: six muffins in a half-dozen box, six eggs cracked for pancakes, six faces on every dice, six strings on a guitar worth a slow strum and count.

Try it together

Dice match: roll a dice, then build the rolled number with grapes or buttons in the same pattern as the dots. Roll a six and the whole room shouts. Then snack subtraction: start with six, eat your way down and count every step.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many grapes? What makes six — five and how many? What shape do the rows make?" Six grapes, one helper finger, two rows of three — past-the-hand counting has begun.

Parent tips

When the hand runs out mid-count, celebrate the moment — "five full, one more!" — because that tiny pause is where place value will someday live. Keep a dice in the snack drawer; it is the cheapest counting teacher ever made.

This lesson pairs with the Six Grapes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Seven Cherries — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson teaches seven through the calendar: seven cherries on the card, seven days in the week. Your child counts seven slowly, splits it four-and-three, and learns why every week ever made has exactly this many days.

What is this?

Seven is six and one more — seven cherries on the card, four on top and three below. Seven is also the number of days it takes to get from one Monday to the next: the whole week in one number.

What does it mean?

Seven is a counting marathon: too big to see at a glance, big enough to wobble. Splitting it into four and three teaches the greatest trick in arithmetic — break a big number into pieces you already know.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sevens: careful touch-counting of seven without losing the place; the four-and-three split from the card's own rows; and the week idea — seven days, and each day has a name.

Why this matters

The week is the first big cycle a child can name, and it is made of sevens. Counting the card's rows teaches decomposition — seeing parts inside numbers — which is how all future mental math will work.

What it teaches

Decomposing numbers (four and three), keeping place in a longer count, sequencing the days of the week, and the first taste of cycles: after seven days, everything starts over.

Words to learn

sevenweekdaystopbottomsplit

Say this to your child

“"Seven cherries, seven days in our week. Four cherries on top, three below — four and three make seven. Every Monday we start counting the week all over again."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Seven cherries — four on top, three below. Seven is how many days are in a whole week!"
  2. Count the top row: one, two, three, four. Count the bottom row: five, six, seven. Four and three, seven in all.
  3. Count the week on fingers: Monday, Tuesday, Wednesday, Thursday, Friday, Saturday, Sunday — seven days, one finger each. Run out of week? That is why it starts over.
  4. Trace the numeral 7 with one finger — down, then across — then draw it in the air. The seven shape is its own small lesson.
  5. Finish with the week plan: pick one thing for each of the next seven days — park day, bath night, Grandma day — one cherry per plan.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 7 stands over seven smiling red cherries with their stems on — four cherries in the top row and three in the bottom row — and the word "cherries" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many cherries? How many on top? How many below?" "What day comes after Sunday?" "How many days until our park day?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Four and three — seven!" "Sunday, then Monday again!" or the planner's line: "Three more sleeps until Saturday."

Out in the real world

The calendar itself is the practice sheet: cross off one day each night and count how many are left in the week. Seven also shows up in nature — seven colors in a rainbow, if the sky cooperates this week.

Try it together

Cherry week: tape seven paper cherries on the wall, one per day, and pull one off every morning — "six cherries left in our week!" Then the split game: drop seven counters in a cup, spill them, and count the groups they land in. Seven always splits somehow.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many cherries? How many days in a week? What two rows make seven?" Seven cherries, seven days, four and three — the week number is learned.

Parent tips

A wobble between six and seven is normal — slow the touching, not the counting voice. Let your child own one weekly ritual (Friday popcorn, Sunday pancakes); waiting for a named day teaches the seven rhythm better than any drill.

This lesson pairs with the Seven Cherries flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Eight Watermelons — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson tames the trickiest counting zone: eight, where fingers run out and pointing races ahead of words. Your child counts eight watermelon slices in two tidy rows, traces the snowman numeral and practices slow, honest counting.

What is this?

Eight is seven and one more — eight watermelon slices in two rows of four. The numeral 8 looks like two circles stacked into a snowman, and the rows on the card split eight into four and four.

What does it mean?

Eight is where counting most often goes wrong: the voice speeds up, the finger stops, and the number comes out tangled. This lesson's whole job is the slow count — one touch, one word, all the way to eight, every time.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three eights: patient touch-counting of eight things in rows; the four-and-four split from the two rows; and the snowman shape — the numeral 8 drawn as one circle balanced on another.

Why this matters

Accurate counting at eight is the gym where counting muscles get strong. The four-and-four split quietly introduces halves and symmetry, and the snowman numeral makes writing eight feel like drawing, which it is.

What it teaches

Row-by-row counting (finish a row, start the next), equal groups as a pre-multiplication idea, numeral formation, and counting stamina — keeping the one-touch-one-word discipline through the longest count so far.

Words to learn

eightsnowmancirclerowsfour and fourslice

Say this to your child

“"Eight slices — four and four, in two neat rows. The 8 looks like a snowman: one circle, then another on top. Let us count slowly, because eight is a long way and slow counting never gets lost."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Eight watermelon slices, two rows of four. And look at the 8 — it is a snowman made of two circles."
  2. Count the top row: one to four. Keep going on the bottom row: five, six, seven, eight. Finish a row, then start the next — that is the pro move.
  3. Draw the snowman in the air: a circle, then a circle on top. Now an 8 lives in the room.
  4. Count a snack into eights: eight berries, eight cereal pieces, laid out in two rows of four exactly like the card.
  5. Slow-motion test: count to eight as slowly as possible, one giant touch per word. Racing is easy; slow is the real skill.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 8 stands over eight smiling watermelon slices with green rind, laid out in two rows of four, and the word "watermelons" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many slices? How many in each row?" "What does the 8 look like to you?" "Can you count to eight slower than a snail?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Four and four — eight!" "A snowman number!" or the proud slow counter's line: "I did not skip a single one."

Out in the real world

Eights crawl and roll through the day: eight legs on a spider or octopus, eight sides if you find a stop sign, eight pieces when a sandwich gets cut in a grid. Spiders are the favorite — count the legs on a picture, never up close.

Try it together

Snowman eights: draw giant 8s in the air with both arms, then lay eight toys in two rows and count the parade. Then the freeze count: clap and count to eight, freeze on eight, and hold it — wobbly freezes get a rematch.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many slices? What does the 8 look like? How many in each row?" Eight slices, a snowman, four and four — the long count is won.

Parent tips

If the count keeps landing on seven or nine, count together in a whisper-slow voice for a few days — accuracy first, speed is free later. Praise the restart, not just the finish: "you lost count and started over like a real counter."

This lesson pairs with the Eight Watermelons flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Nine Peaches — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson counts to the edge of the first decade: nine, one away from ten. Your child counts nine peaches grouped four, three and two, feels the big pause before ten, and learns that counting backwards is just as important as counting up.

What is this?

Nine is eight and one more — nine peaches grouped four, then three, then two on the card. Nine is famous for one thing: it is one short of ten, the number every young counter is aiming for.

What does it mean?

Being "one away" is a powerful mathematical feeling. Nine teaches nearness: how close counting gets you to the finish, and what happens when one more joins. Backwards from nine also makes nine a launching pad, not just a stop.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three nines: careful counting of nine in its funny three groups; the one-more question — "what comes after nine?"; and counting backwards from nine to zero with the voice slowing at the end.

Why this matters

Counting backwards builds the number line in both directions, which subtraction will need later. And the drama of nine-then-TEN makes ten arrive as an event — the loudest, best-earned number of the whole first decade.

What it teaches

Forward and backward counting, anticipation of the next number, group-reading (four, three, two as separate clusters), and impulse control — waiting for the one-more that turns nine into ten.

Words to learn

ninealmostone morebackwardscountdownnext

Say this to your child

“"Nine peaches — four, three and two. Nine is one away from ten. Let us count up, stop at nine, and see who can wait for the ten... and then count backwards like a rocket: nine, eight, seven..."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Nine peaches — four, three and two. Nine is one away from ten. How close is that?"
  2. Count the groups: four, then three, then two — nine peaches in all. Big numbers get easier when they travel in small packs.
  3. Count forward and stop dead after nine. Let the silence stretch. "What comes next?" Let ten be shouted, whispered or exploded — whatever arrives is correct.
  4. Count backwards from nine, voice sinking like a rocket about to launch: nine, eight, seven... and blast off on zero with a jump.
  5. Walk nine steps down the hallway, count them, turn around, count nine back. Same nine, both directions.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 9 stands over nine smiling peaches with leaves, gathered in three groups — four peaches, then three, then two — and the word "peaches" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many peaches? What comes right after nine?" "Can you count backwards from nine?" "How many more peaches would make ten?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Nine! Almost ten!" "TEN comes next!" or the rocket count: "Nine, eight, seven, six... BLAST OFF."

Out in the real world

Nines live on elevators (button nine, top floor of many buildings), in nine-inning games watched on sofas, and in the countdown ritual — rockets, races and microwaves all count backwards, and now your child knows why.

Try it together

The tidy-up countdown: collect nine toys counting up, then send them home counting down — nine to zero, with the last one landing as a touchdown. Then one-more peach: line up nine snacks and let your child add the tenth with full ceremony.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many peaches? What comes after nine? Count backwards for me." Nine peaches, one away, rocket countdown — the door to ten is open.

Parent tips

Do not rush the pause after nine — that silence is your child's brain building the next number. Backwards counting feels silly and that is exactly why it works; join in with the rocket voice and let them out-count you.

This lesson pairs with the Nine Peaches flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Ten Blueberries — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson reaches the summit of first counting: ten, a full pair of hands. Your child counts ten blueberries in two rows of five, matches every berry to a finger and learns that all the teen numbers ahead are built on this one.

What is this?

Ten is nine and one more — ten blueberries in two perfect rows of five. Ten is all ten fingers held up at once, the finish line of first counting and the starting block for everything after.

What does it mean?

Ten is the number the whole number system is built on: every bigger number is "some tens and some more". Seeing ten as two fives — two rows, two hands — plants the idea that big numbers are made of handy, countable parts.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three tens: counting all ten fingers, left hand then right; the two-rows-of-five picture that matches the card and the hands; and the proud feeling of a finished decade — ten is an achievement, not just a word.

Why this matters

Ten is the base of place value, the king of the number line, and the first number worth celebrating hard. A child who owns ten — eyes closed, fingers out — will meet eleven to twenty as "ten and some more" instead of a scary new world.

What it teaches

Two-hand counting, five-plus-five structure, the finished-decade feeling, one-to-one matching between berries and fingers, and celebration stamina — big counts deserve big finishes.

Words to learn

tenblueberriesfingersdoublehandfuldecade

Say this to your child

“"Ten blueberries, ten fingers — two rows of five, two hands of five. Ten is the whole number line in your two hands. Count every finger: one, two, three... all the way to ten!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Ten blueberries — two rows of five. And hold up your hands: ten fingers. Ten is all of them."
  2. Count the top row: one to five. Count the bottom row: six to ten. Then count all ten in one long, careful line.
  3. Match berry to finger: point at each blueberry and raise one finger per berry until both hands stand open. Ten berries, ten fingers — the same ten.
  4. Say the secret: "Everything after ten is ten and some more. You just learned the base camp of all the big numbers."
  5. Celebrate like a finish line: ten claps, ten jumps, ten cheers — one per number, all the way up.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 10 stands over ten smiling blueberries in two neat rows of five, and the word "blueberries" is printed below — the two-row shape matching two open hands of five fingers each.

Ask your child

"How many blueberries? How many rows? How many in each?" "Show me ten fingers. What comes after ten?" "Five and five make...?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Two rows of five!" "Ten — all my fingers!" or the finish-line shout: "I counted all the way to ten!"

Out in the real world

Tens run the world: ten toes to match the fingers, ten pins in bowling, ten dimes in a coin strip, ten numbers on a phone pad. Count change into tens, count stairs in tens, and let the microwave countdown count down from ten one more time.

Try it together

Finger theater: tell a tiny story where each finger wakes up one at a time — ten characters, counted in order, waving goodbye in reverse. Then berry match: scatter ten snacks and race to build two rows of five exactly like the card before eating the evidence.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many berries? Show me ten. What two rows make ten?" Ten blueberries, ten fingers, five and five — the first decade is conquered.

Parent tips

Match berries to fingers physically — the one-to-one touching between card and hands is the lesson, so go slow enough for both to keep up. Make the celebration genuinely huge: a child who remembers reaching ten will sprint toward twenty.

This lesson pairs with the Ten Blueberries flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Eleven Kiwis — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson steps over the ten border: eleven, the first number with two digits. Your child counts eleven kiwi halves as a ten and one more, learns why eleven refuses to sound like "oneteen", and practices the ten-plus-one bridge.

What is this?

Eleven is ten and one more — the first number that needs two numerals to write. On the card, eleven smiling kiwi halves show their green centres in two rows. Count a full ten, then meet the newcomer: eleven.

What does it mean?

Eleven and twelve are the two rebel teens: they do not say "-teen" like the rest. That is why they get their own cards and their own words. Underneath the funny word, the math is simple and loud: ten and one.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three elevens: counting ten and then one more; the word "eleven" as its own word, not a mistake; and the two-numeral idea — the 1 and the 1 side by side mean ten and one more.

Why this matters

Crossing from ten to eleven is the gate into all bigger numbers. If eleven feels like "ten plus a friend", the whole teen decade opens; if it feels like a wall, counting stalls here for months. This lesson makes it a gate.

What it teaches

Two-digit awareness, composing ten and one, flexible counting on from a full ten, and the language insight that number words have history — eleven is old and stubborn and completely learnable.

Words to learn

eleventen and onetwo digitsteenmorebridge

Say this to your child

“"Ten kiwis, and one more — eleven! Eleven is ten and one friend. It does not say oneteen because it is an old, stubborn word, but the math is simple: a full ten and one more."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Eleven kiwis. First we count a whole ten, then one more arrives. Ten and one: eleven!"
  2. Count ten kiwis slowly, then tap the last one with a flourish: "and one more — eleven." The one-more tap is the whole lesson; do it twice.
  3. Look at the numeral: a 1 and a 1 standing together. The first 1 is the ten, the second 1 is the one more. Two digits, one number.
  4. Build it: count out ten blocks, then let your child add exactly one and announce eleven. Take one away, count again — back to ten.
  5. Say the word trick: "Eleven does not say oneteen — it is its own old word, like a number with a grandfather's name."

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 11 stands over eleven smiling cut kiwi halves showing their green centres in two rows, and the word "kiwis" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many kiwis? What is ten and one more?" "Which two digits write eleven?" "What number comes right after ten?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Ten and one — eleven!" "It has two ones!" or the border crossing: "After ten comes eleven, and I know it."

Out in the real world

Elevens sneak into real life: eleven players on a soccer team, the eleventh floor button if you ride high elevators, eleven pipers piping in the song that counts down the twelve days. Sports fans catch this one fast.

Try it together

Ten-plus-one ceremony: any small treat counts out to a full ten, then your child adds the eleventh like a coronation — the one-more gets named out loud. Then race the border: count to ten fast, slow down dramatically, and cross to eleven with one giant step.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many kiwis? What is eleven made of? What word comes after ten?" Eleven kiwis, ten and one, the first teen — the border is crossed.

Parent tips

Do not force "oneteen" logic — eleven is just its own word, and saying so honestly ends the confusion faster than any pattern explanation. The physical one-more tap onto a full ten is worth repeating daily; it is the seed of all place value.

This lesson pairs with the Eleven Kiwis flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Twelve Lemons — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson counts the grown-up dozen: twelve, the number egg boxes and clock faces are built on. Your child counts twelve lemons in three rows of four, hunts dozens in the kitchen and learns ten-and-two-more.

What is this?

Twelve is ten and two more — twelve lemons in three tidy rows of four. Twelve has a famous grown-up name: a dozen. Egg boxes hold a dozen, bakers bake by the dozen, and every clock wears twelve numbers.

What does it mean?

Twelve matters twice: as ten-and-two in the counting system, and as a dozen in daily life — the first "package number" a child can own. The three-rows-of-four layout also shows that the same twelve can be counted in many shapes.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three twelves: counting twelve in rows (four, four, four); the word "dozen" and one real dozen to touch, like an egg box; and the ten-plus-two bridge — a full ten and two friends.

Why this matters

Meeting the dozen early makes shops, kitchens and clocks readable. And counting a dozen in rows is real layout math: three rows of four is the shape of arrays that school math will use for years.

Words to learn

twelvedozenclockrowsten and twobox

Say this to your child

“"Twelve lemons — ten and two more. Twelve is called a dozen: eggs come by the dozen, bakers bake by the dozen, and the clock counts to twelve twice a day. Let us count our own dozen."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Twelve lemons — and twelve has a special name: a dozen. Let us count them in rows."
  2. Count row by row: four, then four more (eight), then four more (twelve). Finish a row, start the next — twelve is too long for one look.
  3. Bridge it: count a full ten lemons, then two more. Ten and two: twelve. Two numerals on top — the 1 for the ten, the 2 for the two.
  4. Open the kitchen dozen: an egg box, a pack of muffin cups, twelve buttons in a jar. Say "a dozen" each time — the word is the treasure.
  5. Clock check: find a clock face and count the numbers around it — one to twelve, twice around the day.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 12 stands over twelve smiling yellow lemons arranged in three rows of four, and the word "lemons" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many lemons? What is a dozen?" "What in our kitchen holds a dozen?" "How many numbers live on a clock?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Ten and two — twelve!" "A dozen eggs!" or the clock report: "The clock goes all the way around to twelve."

Out in the real world

Dozens rule the kitchen and the shop: a dozen eggs, a dozen roses wrapped in paper, doughnuts sold by the dozen. The clock is the free daily rehearsal — every hour, twelve numbers wait to be counted around.

Try it together

Build a dozen: collect twelve of anything — spoons, cars, socks — and arrange them three rows of four, exactly like the lemons, then rearrange into two rows of six and count again. Same twelve, new shape. Then egg-box math: point at each cup and count twelve.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many lemons? What do we call twelve? What are the rows?" Twelve lemons, a dozen, three rows of four — the package number is learned.

Parent tips

The word "dozen" delights children — it sounds like a secret grown-up code, so hand it over proudly. If row-counting tangles, place one finger at the start of each new row; the row-start habit carries through all of school math.

This lesson pairs with the Twelve Lemons flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Thirteen Pineapples — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson disarms the most-tripped-over teen: thirteen. Your child counts thirteen pineapples as ten and three, says the word slowly like a secret, and learns that the "-teen" ending simply means "plus ten".

What is this?

Thirteen is ten and three more — thirteen pineapples with green crowns, grouped five, five and three. The word "thirteen" is famous for tangling young tongues, which is exactly why it gets a whole lesson.

What does it mean?

All the teens end in "-teen" and all the teens mean "ten and some more". Thirteen is where that pattern first becomes words: thir-teen. Saying it in two parts — and counting ten-plus-three — untangles both the word and the number.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three thirteens: the two-part word said slowly (THIR-teen); the ten-and-three count; and the row reading — five and five and three, three packs that make one thirteen.

Why this matters

The stumble at thirteen is normal and fixable. A child who can split thirteen into ten and three has learned the master key to every teen number — and the confidence that tricky words yield to saying them slowly.

What it teaches

Word decomposition (thir + teen), number decomposition (ten + three), reading grouped arrangements, and fluency practice — repetition with rhythm, where the tongue learns the word by walking it.

Words to learn

thirteenteenten and threeslowlygroupscrowns

Say this to your child

“"Thirteen — let us say it like a secret: THIR-teen. It means ten and three more. Every word that ends in teen means ten and something, and thirteen is just the first one that sounds funny."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Thirteen pineapples. This word trips everyone — so we say it slowly: THIR... teen."
  2. Split the word with your hands: one hand for THIR, one for TEEN. Say both parts, then slam them together: thirteen!
  3. Count the math way: a full ten pineapples, then three more. Ten and three — thirteen. Tap the ten, tap the three, say the whole word.
  4. Read the rows: five, five, three. Count each pack, then count them all — the same thirteen wearing three little hats.
  5. Stair practice if you have steps: count thirteen stairs, one word per step. Stairs slow the voice, and a slow voice never stumbles.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 13 stands over thirteen smiling pineapples with green crowns, grouped five in the top row, five in the middle and three below, and the word "pineapples" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many pineapples? Say thirteen slowly — what are its two parts?" "What does teen mean at the end of a number?" "How many in each group?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "THIR-teen — ten and three!" "Five, five, three!" or the proud confession-turned-triumph: "I said it without tripping."

Out in the real world

Thirteen shows up where nobody expects it: thirteen stripes on the flag, thirteen candles on a birthday cake someday, thirteen moons in some years of old farming calendars. The famous unlucky-for-some number becomes friendly when a four-year-old can count it cleanly.

Try it together

The thirteen staircase: stairs, stepping stones or couch cushions — thirteen of anything to walk and count, one number per step. Then teen-word claps: clap once for THIR, once for TEEN, then shout the whole word — the clap splits the word the way the hands did.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many pineapples? What does thirteen mean? Say it in two parts." Thirteen pineapples, ten and three, THIR-teen — the tricky teen is tamed.

Parent tips

Never laugh at the stumble; everyone trips here, including adults learning new languages. Two-part saying plus stair-walking fixes thirteen in under a week. Keep the ten-and-three count separate from the word practice — the tongue and the math learn at different speeds.

This lesson pairs with the Thirteen Pineapples flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Fourteen Raspberries — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson catches the teen pattern red-handed: fourteen, ten and four. Your child counts fourteen raspberries, says the ten-plus-four recipe out loud, and discovers that from here to twenty, every number follows the same trick.

What is this?

Fourteen is ten and four more — fourteen raspberries grouped five, five and four. The word says it plainly: four-teen. And fourteen hides a second treasure: a fortnight, two whole weeks, fourteen days.

What does it mean?

Fourteen is the first teen where the word and the math match perfectly — four plus teen. Once a child hears that recipe, fifteen through nineteen arrive as a march instead of a struggle. Fourteen is the pattern lesson.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three fourteens: the ten-and-four count said as a recipe; the fortnight idea — fourteen days, two weeks; and group-reading the card: five, five, four.

Why this matters

Naming the ten-plus-more pattern at fourteen is the whole point of the teens. From here, each new number is practice, not novelty — the pattern does the teaching, and the child starts predicting the next number before you say it.

What it teaches

Pattern recognition across numbers, the ten-plus-n recipe spoken aloud, counting grouped rows to fourteen, and prediction — guessing what comes next and being right.

Words to learn

fourteenraspberriespatternrecipegroupspredict

Say this to your child

“"Fourteen — ten and four more. The word says it: FOUR-teen. And a fortnight? Fourteen days, two whole weeks. From now on, every teen number is ten and some more — you know the trick."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Fourteen raspberries — say the word slowly and listen: FOUR-teen. It tells you the recipe: ten and four more!"
  2. Count ten raspberries, then four more, pointing as you go: "Ten... and four... fourteen."
  3. Read the packs: five, five, four. Count each group, then all fourteen. Big numbers travel in packs.
  4. Tell the fortnight secret: "A fortnight is fourteen days — two whole weeks in one word. Two Mondays away: that is a fortnight."
  5. Predict: "Fifteen comes next. What do you think it will be? Ten and... five!" Let the pattern finish the sentence.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 14 stands over fourteen smiling red raspberries, grouped five in the top row, five in the middle and four below, and the word "raspberries" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many raspberries? What is fourteen made of?" "What does the word fourteen tell you?" "How long is a fortnight?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Ten and four — fourteen!" "A fortnight is two weeks!" or the pattern prediction: "Fifteen will be ten and five!"

Out in the real world

Fortnights organize family life: a fortnight until the grandparents visit, holiday countdowns in weeks and days. Raspberries themselves count at the market — a punnet held open for a quick five-and-five-and-four count.

Try it together

Recipe numbers: say any teen number as a recipe and build it — ten blocks plus four blocks, stacked apart, counted together. Then the fortnight chain: paper-link fourteen days, tear one daily, and count what is left each morning toward the big day.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many raspberries? Say the recipe. What is a fortnight?" Fourteen, ten and four, two weeks — the pattern is caught.

Parent tips

This is the lesson to be loud about the pattern — children who catch the ten-plus recipe at fourteen glide to twenty alone. If they start predicting fifteen and sixteen correctly, celebrate like they invented arithmetic, because for them, they just did.

This lesson pairs with the Fourteen Raspberries flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Fifteen Mangoes — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson counts fifteen the efficient way: three rows of five. Your child counts fifteen mangoes row by row, says the ten-and-five recipe and learns that counting by fives is the first counting shortcut.

What is this?

Fifteen is ten and five more — fifteen mangoes in three rows of five. It is also the halfway house of the teens, and the first number that begs to be counted in fives instead of ones.

What does it mean?

Counting by ones to fifteen is a long walk; counting by rows is a shortcut. Three fives make fifteen, and that insight — equal groups make big numbers — is the doorway to skip counting and, much later, multiplication.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three fifteens: the ten-and-five recipe; row counting — five, five, five; and the halfway feeling: fifteen is exactly midway between ten and twenty.

Why this matters

Fives are the friendliest grouping for young counters — they match hands. A child who counts fifteen as three rows of five is doing real structural math with fruit, and the halfway landmark gives the teens a middle they can aim at.

What it teaches

Skip counting by fives (seeds of it), equal-groups reading, halfway landmarks on the number line, and the ten-plus-five recipe — one more teen number absorbed into the pattern.

Words to learn

fifteenhalfwayrows of fiveshortcutten and fivemiddle

Say this to your child

“"Fifteen mangoes — ten and five more, or three rows of five. Fifteen is the middle of the teens, halfway from ten to twenty. Counting by rows is the counting shortcut."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Fifteen mangoes in three rows of five. We could count one by one... or we could take the shortcut."
  2. Count the slow way once: all fifteen, one touch per mango. Respect the long walk.
  3. Take the shortcut: count each row — five, five, five. Then count all: fifteen. Same answer, half the breath.
  4. Say the recipe: ten and five more. Count a full ten, then the last row of five — fifteen.
  5. Find the middle: "Fifteen is exactly halfway between ten and twenty." Hop three times: ten, fifteen, twenty — short hop, big landmark.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 15 stands over fifteen smiling yellow mangoes with leaves, arranged in three rows of five, and the word "mangoes" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many mangoes? How many rows and how many in each?" "What is ten and five more?" "What number is halfway between ten and twenty?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Five, five, five — fifteen!" "Ten and five!" or the landmark claim: "Fifteen is the middle one."

Out in the real world

Fifteens tick in quiet places: fifteen minutes is a quarter of an hour (the kitchen timer proves it), fifteen items in a long shop list, fifteen steps to the letterbox. The timer is the star — one ding per quarter hour all afternoon.

Try it together

Row builder: deal fifteen snacks into three rows of five exactly like the card, count by rows, then eat a row and count what remains — ten! Two rows of five are just ten wearing a snack outfit. Then hop the landmark: jump from ten to fifteen to twenty, shouting the landings.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many mangoes? What are the rows? What is the recipe?" Fifteen, three rows of five, ten and five — the halfway number is claimed.

Parent tips

Let them count by ones first — the shortcut only feels like a shortcut after the long walk. If a row gets sixteen, count again together and shrug; the rows make errors easy to see and easy to fix, which is why they are here.

This lesson pairs with the Fifteen Mangoes flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Sixteen Coconuts — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson builds the first square: sixteen, four rows of four. Your child counts sixteen coconuts, lays them into a square block, and learns that some numbers make perfect shapes — and shapes make counting easy.

What is this?

Sixteen is ten and six more — sixteen coconuts on the card in three rows of five plus one more. But sixteen has a second, magic shape: four rows of four make a perfect square. Same sixteen, two outfits.

What does it mean?

Sixteen is the first square number a child can actually build. Seeing a number as a shape — not just a heap — is structural math: the same sixteen can be a row of five plus more, or a tidy square, and both are true at once.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three sixteens: the ten-and-six recipe; the square build — four rows of four; and the flexible idea that one number can wear different shapes without changing.

Why this matters

Square numbers recur all through school math, and meeting one at coconut scale makes it concrete. Rearranging sixteen from the card's layout into a square also teaches the deepest counting truth: moving things does not change how many there are.

Words to learn

sixteensquareblocksgridcornersrebuild

Say this to your child

“"Sixteen coconuts — ten and six more. Now the magic part: build the same sixteen with blocks, four lines of four, and a square appears. A number that doubles as a shape!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Sixteen coconuts. Count them with me — then we will discover the secret shape of sixteen."
  2. Count all sixteen, ten-and-six style: a full ten, then six more. The recipe never fails.
  3. Now the magic: gather sixteen blocks or buttons and build four rows of four. Count the rows, count the square — sixteen! Draw around it with one finger: a square.
  4. Compare shapes: the card's layout and your square. Both are sixteen. Rearranging never changes the count — that is a counting law.
  5. Walk the square: count four blocks across, four down, four across, four up — sixteen steps around the border of a number.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 16 stands over sixteen smiling brown coconuts, arranged in three rows of five with one more coconut beside them, and the word "coconuts" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many coconuts? What is ten and six?" "Can you build sixteen as a square?" "Does the count change if we rearrange them?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Four rows of four!" "It is a square number!" or the law discovery: "It is still sixteen even when we move them."

Out in the real world

Sixteens hold up buildings and games: a four-by-four window grid, sixteen squares on part of a chessboard, sixteen crayons in a small box. Windows are everywhere — four across, four down, sixteen panes, free and daily.

Try it together

Square builder: sixteen blocks, four rows of four — then break one corner and count: fifteen! The broken square proves the count. Then the shape hunt: find anything arranged in four rows of four, count it, and crown it a sixteen.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many coconuts? What shape can sixteen make? Does moving them change the count?" Sixteen, four rows of four, never changes — the square number is built.

Parent tips

Let the rearranging get silly — lines, circles, towers — and count every time: always sixteen. That repetition is the conservation lesson, and it lands better through play than through any explanation. Keep the coconut squishiness in the words: numbers are bendy shapes.

This lesson pairs with the Sixteen Coconuts flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Seventeen Apples — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson builds counting stamina: seventeen, deep in the teens. Your child counts seventeen apples as ten and seven, learns where long counts usually wobble and picks up the restart-from-ten rescue trick.

What is this?

Seventeen is ten and seven more — seventeen apples grouped six, six and five on the card. Seventeen is far enough along that long counts get tired: most counting wobbles happen between fifteen and eighteen.

What does it mean?

Long counts need a rescue plan. When a seventeen-count tangles, restarting from one wastes all that work — restarting from ten saves it. That little trick, counting on from a known landmark, is a genuine math strategy hiding in a snack.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three seventeens: the ten-and-seven recipe; the wobble map — most stumbles land between fifteen and eighteen; and the rescue — when lost, go back to ten and count on.

Why this matters

Endurance counting is a real skill: the discipline to keep one-touch-one-word going for seventeen steps. The restart-from-ten trick teaches that landmarks are safe harbors — the same habit that will one day become adding on a number line.

Words to learn

seventeensteadywobblerestartlandmarkten and seven

Say this to your child

“"Seventeen apples — ten and seven. Long counts wobble near the end sometimes, and that is fine: when we get lost, we jump back to ten and count on. Ten is a safe harbor."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Seventeen apples — ten and seven more. This is a long count, so we count like professionals: steady and slow."
  2. Recipe count: a full ten apples, then seven more, tapping each one. Ten and seven: seventeen.
  3. Read the groups: six, six, five. Count each pack, then the whole seventeen — big numbers in little packs.
  4. Practice the rescue: count and "accidentally" lose your place near sixteen. Laugh, and show the trick — "back to ten! Ten... eleven, twelve..." Counting on from ten, not from one.
  5. Clap-count to seventeen with a metronome voice — steady as a clock. If it tangles, restart from ten together.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 17 stands over seventeen smiling red apples, grouped six in the top row, six in the middle and five below, and the word "apples" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many apples? What is ten and seven more?" "Where do long counts usually get tangled?" "What is the rescue trick when we lose count?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Ten and seven — seventeen!" "Back to ten and count on!" or the steady-counter's badge: "I counted all seventeen with no wobble."

Out in the real world

Seventeens turn up on big number lines: bus routes, house numbers on a long street, calendar dates — walk past date seventeen every month. Number the steps of a staircase with sticky notes and let seventeen be the summit of the morning climb.

Try it together

Steady-hand count: seventeen coins into a jar, one per second, metronome-steady — wobble means back to ten, not back to one. Then apple pack relay: sort seventeen toys into packs of six, six and five like the card, count each pack, then the whole lot.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many apples? Say the recipe. What do we do when the count tangles?" Seventeen, ten and seven, restart from ten — the steady count is trained.

Parent tips

Do the fake-wobble rescue yourself first — children adore catching a grown-up losing count, and the trick teaches itself while they laugh. Never demand perfection at seventeen; demand the restart habit, and perfection arrives on its own later.

This lesson pairs with the Seventeen Apples flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Eighteen Bananas — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson counts eighteen by its rows: three rows of six. Your child counts eighteen bananas the slow way and the row way, feels equal groups doing the work, and stands one step from the last teen.

What is this?

Eighteen is ten and eight more — eighteen bananas in three rows of six. The rows are the lesson: six, six and six land exactly on eighteen, the first time equal groups march all the way to a number this big.

What does it mean?

Three sixes making eighteen is equal-group math in plain sight — the great-grandparent of times tables. Reading a number by its rows, instead of one by one, is the fastest counting growth available at this age.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three eighteens: the ten-and-eight recipe; the row count — six, six, six; and the neighbor awareness: eighteen is one away from nineteen, two away from twenty.

Why this matters

Equal groups quietly introduce multiplication years before the word appears. And eighteen's place — second-to-last teen — makes it the natural stopping point to look back at ten and ahead to twenty, tying the whole decade together.

Words to learn

eighteenrowssix and six and sixequalgroupsalmost

Say this to your child

“"Eighteen bananas — three rows of six. Six, six, and six again make eighteen. Ten and eight works too. We are one step from the last teen number — listen to how close twenty sounds."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Eighteen bananas in three rows of six. First the long way, then the clever way."
  2. Long way: count all eighteen, one touch per banana, steady voice. The long walk earns the shortcut.
  3. Clever way: count one row — six. Second row — six more, twelve. Third row — six more, eighteen! Six and six and six.
  4. Recipe check: ten and eight more. Count a full ten, then the remaining eight — same eighteen, two ways, one number.
  5. Look both ways: "Eighteen is one away from nineteen and two away from twenty." Count those tiny hops — the end of the teens is near.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 18 stands over eighteen smiling yellow bananas arranged in three rows of six, and the word "bananas" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many bananas? How many rows, how many in each?" "What is ten and eight more?" "How far is eighteen from twenty?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Six, six, six — eighteen!" "Ten and eight!" or the lookout's call: "Nineteen is next, then twenty!"

Out in the real world

Eighteens sit in grown-up number land: the eighteenth birthday (the biggest one on the calendar horizon), eighteen holes on a golf course, house number eighteen on the walk to school. The birthday is the headline — eighteen years feels impossibly far and hugely exciting.

Try it together

Row dealer: deal eighteen cards or snacks into three rows of six exactly like the card, count by rows, then remove a row and count — twelve! Rebuild and count again. Then the two-hop game: from eighteen, hop to nineteen, hop to twenty — two hops to the summit.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many bananas? What do the rows say? What comes after eighteen?" Eighteen, six and six and six, nineteen next — the rows are counted.

Parent tips

Counting by rows may lose the child on "twelve" as a running total — that is fine; say "six more makes twelve" slowly and tap it out. The point today is the shape of equal groups, not memorizing anything. Eighteen is a happy, almost-done number — let it sound that way.

This lesson pairs with the Eighteen Bananas flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Nineteen Apricots — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson arrives at the edge of the teens: nineteen, one away from twenty. Your child counts nineteen apricots as ten and nine, holds the famous pause, and lets the whole family shout the twenty that ends the set.

What is this?

Nineteen is ten and nine more — nineteen apricots grouped seven, seven and five. It is the last teen number: after nineteen, the twenties begin, and twenty itself is waiting like a summit at the end of a climb.

What does it mean?

Nineteen's job is anticipation. The count climbs to nineteen and stops — and the pause before "twenty" is the most dramatic moment in first counting. Waiting for a number you can feel coming is real mathematical intuition.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three nineteens: the ten-and-nine recipe; the last-teen fact — after nineteen comes twenty; and the pause skill — stopping at the end of a count and letting the next number arrive on purpose.

Why this matters

Holding a pause before a known answer builds prediction and self-control in one move. Nineteen also completes the teen pattern one last time — ten and nine — so the whole decade can be reviewed from this summit view.

Words to learn

nineteenlastpausealmosttwentysummit

Say this to your child

“"Nineteen apricots — ten and nine, the last teen of all. Count to nineteen and stop... and hold... and hold... TWENTY! You just climbed the whole teen decade."”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Nineteen apricots — the LAST teen. Ten and nine more, and then... well. You will see."
  2. Recipe count: a full ten, then nine more, tapping steadily. Ten and nine: nineteen.
  3. Read the packs: seven, seven, five. Count each group, then all nineteen — three packs, one number.
  4. The famous pause: count to nineteen and stop dead. Let the silence grow as long as it can bear. When "TWENTY!" arrives, celebrate it like a goal scored.
  5. Summit view: count the teen decade quickly — eleven, twelve, thirteen... nineteen — and bow to the audience. The teens are done.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 19 stands over nineteen smiling orange apricots, grouped seven in the top row, seven in the middle and five below, and the word "apricots" is printed below.

Ask your child

"How many apricots? What is ten and nine?" "Which number comes after nineteen?" "Why did we stop and wait at nineteen?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Ten and nine — nineteen!" "Nineteen is the last teen!" or the exploded summit: "TWENTY comes next — I have been waiting!"

Out in the real world

Nineteens live at the top of the teens: house number nineteen, the nineteenth of the month on every calendar, nineteen stairs if your staircase is tall enough. The calendar corner-flip to the nineteenth is a tiny monthly rehearsal nobody skips.

Try it together

The twenty ceremony: nineteen snacks counted out loud, one held dramatically above the plate... and dropped as the twentieth with a family shout of TWENTY. Then teen decade relay: run the teens in order, and the runner who lands on nineteen freezes while the next shouts twenty.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many apricots? What comes after nineteen? What is the recipe?" Nineteen, ten and nine, twenty — the last teen is done.

Parent tips

Hold the pause longer than feels polite — anticipation is doing heavy teaching work while everyone stays quiet. If your child shouts twenty early every time, whisper-count the teens backward from nineteen; the pause returns once the routine feels new again.

This lesson pairs with the Nineteen Apricots flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).

LEARNING PATH LESSON · NUMBERS, COUNTING & EARLY MATH · AGES 4–5 YEARS

Twenty Figs — a step-by-step lesson for grown-up and child

This lesson crowns the whole set: twenty, two full tens. Your child counts twenty figs in four rows of five, takes twenty apart and rebuilds it, and celebrates the summit — a wall-worthy finish to a month of counting.

What is this?

Twenty is two tens — twenty figs in four neat rows of five. It is the biggest number on the whole journey, the second finished decade, and the number every finger-and-toe counter has been walking toward.

What does it mean?

Twenty is where big numbers start to be SEEABLE: two tens, four fives, one big block of fruit. Taking twenty apart — cover a row, count what is left — and rebuilding it teaches that numbers are built things, and built things can be understood.

What does the child need to know?

Your child needs three twenties: the two-tens recipe; the row reading — four rows of five; and the take-apart move — covering some figs, counting the rest, uncovering and counting all.

Why this matters

Twenty completes the journey from a single apple to a structured number you can take apart. That take-apart-and-rebuild move is exactly what arithmetic will ask forever — and reaching twenty earns the celebration that makes counting something a child wants to return to.

Words to learn

twentytwo tensrows of fivetake apartrebuildsummit

Say this to your child

“"Twenty figs — two tens, four rows of five. We can count it, cover it, take it apart and rebuild it — twenty always comes back. You counted all the way from one apple to twenty figs. That is a mountain!"”

Step by step

  1. Show the card: "Twenty figs — the biggest number on the whole journey! Two full tens, four rows of five. Let us climb it."
  2. Count by rows: five, ten, fifteen, twenty — land on each row-end with a little drumroll. The row landings ARE counting by fives.
  3. Recipe count: a full ten figs, then ten more. Two tens: twenty. Say it both ways — rows and tens.
  4. Take it apart: cover one row of five and count what is left — fifteen! Uncover, count again — twenty. Numbers can be dismantled and rebuilt without fear.
  5. Summit celebration: hang this card highest, or pin all twenty cards across a wall in order and walk the number line from one to twenty like a parade.

Look closer at the picture

On this card a big black numeral 20 stands over twenty smiling purple figs arranged in four neat rows of five, and the word "figs" is printed below — the summit card of the whole set.

Ask your child

"How many figs? What are the four rows? What is twenty made of — how many tens?" "If I cover one row, how many are left?"

What your child can say or do

Your child might say: "Two tens — twenty!" "Five, ten, fifteen, twenty!" or the summit declaration: "I counted all the way to twenty."

Out in the real world

Twenties run the house: twenty pegs on the washing line, twenty stairs, the number twenty bus, twenty minutes of bedtime story. Deal twenty crackers at a party and the count feeds everybody — numbers this big have jobs.

Try it together

Number line parade: lay all twenty cards across the floor in order and walk them — one step, one number, a full march from one to twenty. Then take-apart theater: cover different rows of the fig card and race to count what remains — fifteen, ten, five — then uncover and rebuild the twenty.

Understanding check

Ask: "How many figs? What is twenty made of? Show me how to take it apart." Twenty figs, two tens, four rows of five — the summit is claimed, and the whole set is learned.

Parent tips

The row landings (five, ten, fifteen, twenty) are skip counting in disguise — say them with a little bounce and the rhythm plants itself. And make the wall parade permanent for a few days: walking their own number line every morning is the victory lap this summit deserves.

This lesson pairs with the Twenty Figs flashcard in the library — print it, show it, keep it on the fridge. Back to Numbers, Counting & Early Math (Class 35).
